implementation_notes: The Kotlin module of Resilience4j wraps the Java CircuitBreaker with coroutine extensions: executeSuspendFunction { ... } runs a suspend function under the breaker, decorateSuspendFunction { ... } returns a reusable suspend function, and Flow gets a .circuitBreaker(breaker) operator; the same module provides extensions for RateLimiter, Retry, TimeLimiter and semaphore bulkheads only (no ThreadPoolBulkhead). The documentation is explicit that decorating a suspend function with a CircuitBreaker adds no additional suspension points - the switch to suspension happens for RateLimiter and Retry, which use delay() - so the breaker itself never parks a coroutine: only admission, counting and the cooldown deadline are involved, and a cancelled scope releases the half-open permission without recording an outcome. Use the plain Java API when a team prefers no extensions, and only hand-roll a suspend state machine when Resilience4j cannot be added at all, because it would re-implement the same AtomicReference state machine.
pitfalls: CallNotPermittedException arrives as an ordinary exception inside the coroutine, so map it to a fallback before it escapes and cancels sibling coroutines in a structured-concurrency scope.
A blocking call (JDBC, blocking HTTP) inside executeSuspendFunction still occupies a dispatcher thread; confine it with a limited-parallelism view or a blocking-friendly dispatcher.
One CircuitBreaker instance per dependency: instances built with ofDefaults are cheap but sharing one across services merges their failure domains.
Flow operators apply in chain order, so retry applied before circuitBreaker retries rejections unless the retry predicate excludes the open-circuit error.
